stem: A point charge of +3.0 nC sits at the center of a closed cube with 0.10 m edges. What is the net electric flux through the entire surface of the cube?
A closed surface encloses a +5.0 μC charge and a −2.0 μC charge. A +6.0 μC charge lies just outside the surface. What is the net electric flux through the surface?

A closed surface encloses a +4.0 μC charge at its center. A +4.0 μC charge sits outside the surface. The inside charge is moved to a spot near the surface (still inside), and the outside charge is moved closer to the surface (still outside). What happens to the net electric flux through the surface?
criteria: A. It stays the same only if the inside charge returns to the center
B. It increases, because the field at the surface is stronger
D. It decreases, because part of the surface is now closer to the charge

stem: A sphere has a uniform volume charge density ρ₀ = 2.0 μC/m³ inside it. What charge lies within a concentric sphere of radius r = 0.10 m inside the charged region?
A spherically symmetric charge distribution has volume charge density ρ(r) = αr, with α = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ C/m⁴, for r from 0 to 0.50 m. What charge lies within r = 0.20 m?
A spherical region has zero charge density for r < 0.10 m and a uniform density ρ = 4.0 μC/m³ for 0.10 m < r < 0.30 m. What charge lies within a concentric sphere of radius 0.20 m?
In one region the electric potential is V(x) = (5.0 V/m)x + 2.0 V. What is the x-component of the electric field at x = 1.0 m?
The electric potential along the x-axis is V(x) = 3.0x² − 4.0x, with V in volts and x in meters. What is E_x at x = 2.0 m?
The potential along the x-axis consists of straight-line segments: V = 10 V at x = 0, V = 2 V at x = 0.20 m, and V = 11 V at x = 0.50 m. Which choice gives E_x in each segment?
criteria: A. +10 V/m for 0 < x < 0.20 m, then +22 V/m for 0.20 m < x < 0.50 m
B. (correct) +40 V/m for 0 < x < 0.20 m, then −30 V/m for 0.20 m < x < 0.50 m
D. +30 V/m for 0 < x < 0.20 m, then −40 V/m for 0.20 m < x < 0.50 m

stem: In a certain region of space the electric potential has the same value, 8.0 V, at every point. What is the electric field in that region?
criteria: B. 8.0 V/m in the direction of increasing x
C. Nonzero and directed toward the lower-potential side
D. −(8.0 V)/x, falling off with position

stem: The potential along the x-axis is V(x) = 4.0x² − 16x + 12, with V in volts and x in meters. At what position is E_x equal to zero?
A smooth potential V(x) has a local maximum at x = 1.0 m and a local minimum at x = 3.0 m. Which statement about E_x is correct?
criteria: A. E_x is zero at both points and negative between them
B. E_x is most positive at x = 1.0 m and most negative at x = 3.0 m
C. E_x is nonzero at both points because V is not zero there
D. (correct) E_x is zero at both points and positive between them

stem: The plates of a parallel-plate capacitor, with nothing between them, are pulled apart until their separation is three times the original value. The plate area is unchanged. The capacitance becomes
criteria: A. three times its original value
B. (correct) one-third of its original value
C. unchanged, since the area is the same
D. one-ninth of its original value

stem: A parallel-plate capacitor has rectangular plates 0.040 m by 0.050 m separated by 1.0 mm of vacuum. Neglecting edge effects, what is its capacitance?
Capacitor 1 has circular plates of radius R separated by d. Capacitor 2 has circular plates of radius 2R separated by 3d. Both are vacuum-filled. What is C₂/C₁, neglecting edge effects?
A 10 μF capacitor is charged until the potential difference across it is 6.0 V. How much energy is stored in the capacitor?

A parallel-plate capacitor is charged to charge Q and then disconnected from the battery. The plates are slowly pulled apart until their separation is twice the original value. The energy stored in the capacitor is now
criteria: A. four times its original value
D. unchanged, because the charge is fixed

stem: A 4.0 μF capacitor already has a potential difference of 2.0 V across it. How much additional energy must be supplied to charge it until the potential difference is 5.0 V?
A solid copper sphere is given a net positive charge and then left alone until all charge motion has stopped. What is the electric field at a point inside the copper, well below its surface?
criteria: A. Equal to the field just outside the surface
B. Nonzero, because the excess charge repels itself
C. Directed radially outward and growing with distance from the center

stem: A neutral solid metal slab is placed in a uniform external electric field of magnitude 4.0 × 10³ N/C directed along +x. After the charges in the slab finish rearranging, what is the magnitude of the net electric field within the metal of the slab?

A solid conducting sphere of radius 0.30 m carries a net charge of +6.0 nC and is in electrostatic equilibrium. Taking V = 0 infinitely far away, what is the electric potential at the center of the sphere? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
Two point charges are held fixed in place. If the distance between them is cut to one-half of its original value, the magnitude of the electric force between them becomes
Two small spheres carry charges of +3.0 μC and +5.0 μC and are 0.30 m apart. What is the magnitude of the electric force each sphere exerts on the other? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)

Two fixed point charges repel each other with a force of magnitude 12 N when they are 0.20 m apart. One charge is then doubled and the separation is increased to 0.60 m. What is the new force magnitude?
A small object carrying a positive charge sits at the origin. At a point P located due east of it, the electric field due to this object points
criteria: A. (correct) east, away from the object
C. north, perpendicular to the line joining P and the object
D. west or east, depending on the sign of the test charge used

stem: A point charge of −4.0 nC sits at the origin. What are the magnitude and direction of the electric field at a point 0.20 m from the charge? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
A charge of +2.0 μC is at x = 0 and a charge of −2.0 μC is at x = 0.40 m. What are the magnitude and direction of the net electric field at x = 0.20 m? (k = 9.0 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²)
criteria: B. 2.2 × 10⁵ N/C, toward the negative charge
C. 4.5 × 10⁵ N/C, toward the negative charge
D. (correct) 9.0 × 10⁵ N/C, toward the negative charge

stem: A thin rod of length 0.40 m carries charge distributed uniformly along its length with linear density λ = 5.0 nC/m. What is the total charge on the rod?
A rod lies along the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 0.50 m. Its linear charge density increases with position as λ(x) = ax, where a = 4.0 μC/m². What is the total charge on the rod?
A thin arc of radius 0.30 m spans the angles from θ = −π/2 to θ = +π/2 about the x-axis. Its linear charge density is λ(θ) = λ₀ cos θ with λ₀ = 5.0 nC/m. What is the total charge on the arc?

A uniform electric field of magnitude 200 N/C passes through a flat surface of area 0.50 m². The normal to the surface makes an angle of 60° with the field. What is the electric flux through the surface?
A square loop of side 0.10 m is placed in a uniform electric field of magnitude 5.0 × 10³ N/C so that the plane of the loop is parallel to the field lines. What is the electric flux through the loop?

A uniform electric field has components Eₓ = 300 N/C and E_y = 400 N/C. A flat surface of area 0.20 m² lies in the xz-plane, with its area vector pointing along +y. What is the electric flux through the surface?
A spherical Gaussian surface encloses a +3.0 nC point charge. A second point charge of +5.0 nC lies outside the sphere. What is the net electric flux through the sphere? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²))
A point charge sits just outside one face of an imaginary closed cube, not touching it. What is the total electric flux through the entire surface of the cube due to this outside charge?
criteria: A. Negative, because the field is strongest at the nearest face
B. q/ε₀, because the charge’s field passes through the surface
C. (correct) Zero, because each field line entering the cube also leaves it
D. Positive, because the field at the near face points into the cube

stem: A charge +Q lies inside a closed surface. A charge −Q is then placed just outside the surface. Compared with the situation before the second charge was added, which statement is correct?
criteria: A. The net flux becomes zero because the total charge is zero
B. The net flux and the field at every surface point are both unchanged
C. (correct) The net flux is unchanged, but the field at points on the surface changes
D. The net flux becomes negative because the new charge is negative

stem: A positive point charge and a negative point charge of equal magnitude are held a short distance apart. An external agent slowly pulls them farther apart. How does the electric potential energy of the two-charge system change?
criteria: A. It stays constant, because the charge magnitudes do not change
C. It decreases, because the charges move away from each other
D. It decreases, because the attractive force does negative work

stem: A +3.0 μC point charge and a −2.0 μC point charge are initially 0.30 m apart. They are moved until they are 0.10 m apart. What is the change in the electric potential energy of the pair?

Three point charges are fixed on a line: +2.0 μC at x = 0, −1.0 μC at x = 0.10 m, and +2.0 μC at x = 0.20 m. What is the total electric potential energy of this three-charge system, taking zero energy when the charges are infinitely far apart?
Take the electric potential to be zero infinitely far away. What is the electric potential 0.30 m from an isolated point charge of +5.0 nC?
At a distance of 0.10 m from a point charge, the electric potential is −120 V (zero at infinity). What is the potential at 0.40 m from the same charge?
A fixed point charge of +2.0 nC produces the radial field E = kq/r² directed outward. Evaluating ΔV = −∫E dr along a radial path, how much higher is the potential at r = 0.10 m than at r = 0.40 m?
A small grain carrying a negative charge is released from rest in a region with a static electric field, and no other forces act on it. As the grain speeds up, it moves toward points of
criteria: A. lower potential and higher potential energy
B. higher potential and higher potential energy
C. lower potential and lower potential energy
D. (correct) higher potential and lower potential energy

stem: A +3.0 μC charge is moved by an external agent from point A, where the electric potential is +50 V, to point B, where the potential is +20 V. What is the change in the charge's electric potential energy?

A particle with charge −2.0 μC and mass 3.0×10⁻⁴ kg is released from rest at point P, where the electric potential is +100 V. Only the static electric field acts on it. What is its speed when it reaches point Q, where the potential is +400 V?
criteria: D. Zero; the particle stays at rest

stem: A charged solid metal object sits in electrostatic equilibrium. Why must the electric field just outside its surface be perpendicular to the surface?
criteria: A. Electric field lines always cross every surface at right angles
B. Excess charge spreads uniformly over any conductor, and uniform charge gives only a perpendicular field
C. A steady surface current cancels any part of the field along the surface
D. (correct) A component along the surface would push charges along it, so equilibrium allows none

stem: An uncharged metal sphere is placed in a uniform electric field that points in the +x direction and is allowed to reach electrostatic equilibrium. At the point on the sphere's surface farthest in the −x direction, the electric field just outside the surface is
criteria: A. (correct) Perpendicular to the surface, pointing toward the sphere (+x)
B. Zero, because the field inside the metal is zero
C. Perpendicular to the surface, pointing away from the sphere (−x)
D. Tangent to the surface, pointing along +y

stem: A charged conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has a broad flat face and a sharp pointed tip. Which statement about the electric field just outside its surface is correct?
criteria: A. Perpendicular at the flat face but tilted along the surface near the tip
B. Perpendicular everywhere, and stronger at the flat face because it holds more total charge
C. (correct) Perpendicular everywhere, and stronger at the tip than at the flat face
D. Perpendicular everywhere, and equal at the tip and the flat face because the surface is at one potential

stem: A parallel-plate capacitor is charged by a battery, which is then disconnected. A dielectric with κ = 4 is slipped in to fill the space between the plates completely. The energy stored in the capacitor becomes
criteria: A. one-sixteenth of its original value
C. (correct) one-fourth of its original value
D. four times its original value

stem: A 2.0 μF parallel-plate capacitor is connected to a 6.0 V battery and stays connected. A dielectric with κ = 2.5 is then inserted to fill the gap completely. What is the energy stored in the capacitor after insertion?

A 4.0 μF parallel-plate capacitor is charged to 100 V by a battery, and the battery is then removed. A dielectric with κ = 4 is inserted to fill the gap completely. By how much does the stored energy change?
A very long straight wire carries a uniform linear charge density of +4.0 nC/m. Using Gauss's law, what is the magnitude of the electric field 0.20 m from the wire?
A very long solid cylinder of radius 0.10 m carries a uniform volume charge density of +5.0 μC/m³. What is the electric field magnitude at a point inside the cylinder, 0.040 m from its axis?

A very long straight wire with uniform linear charge density +6.0 nC/m lies along the axis of a long thin cylindrical shell of radius 0.20 m. The shell carries a uniform charge of −12 nC per meter of length. What are the magnitude and direction of the electric field at 0.50 m from the axis?
criteria: A. (correct) 216 N/C, directed toward the axis
B. 432 N/C, directed toward the axis
C. 648 N/C, directed away from the axis
D. 216 N/C, directed away from the axis

stem: A very long straight thin rod carries a uniform linear charge density λ = 3.0 nC/m. A cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius 0.40 m is coaxial with the rod and has a length of 0.50 m. What is the charge enclosed by this Gaussian surface?

A solid insulating sphere of radius 0.10 m carries a total charge of +8.0 µC spread uniformly through its volume. A concentric spherical Gaussian surface has radius 0.050 m. What charge does this Gaussian surface enclose?

A spherical Gaussian surface of radius 0.20 m is concentric with both. What charge does the Gaussian surface enclose?
Along the x-axis the electric potential is V(x) = 40 − 8.0x², with V in volts and x in meters. What is the x-component of the electric field at x = 2.0 m?

The electric potential along the x-axis is constant at 10 V for x < 2.0 m, decreases linearly to 4.0 V between x = 2.0 m and x = 5.0 m, and is constant at 4.0 V for x > 5.0 m. What is the electric field in the region 2.0 m < x < 5.0 m?
criteria: A. Zero, because V is nonzero there

stem: In a region of the x-axis the electric field component is E_x = 3.0x², with E_x in V/m and x in meters. What is the potential difference V(2.0 m) − V(0)?
Two identical point charges of +2.0 µC are fixed 0.60 m apart in vacuum. Take V = 0 at infinity. What are the magnitude of the electric field and the electric potential at the midpoint between them?

A charge of +6.0 nC and a charge of −2.0 nC are fixed 0.40 m apart in vacuum. Take V = 0 at infinity. What are the magnitude and direction of the electric field, and the electric potential, at the midpoint of the line joining them?
criteria: A. 9.0×10² N/C toward the −2.0 nC charge; 3.6×10² V
B. (correct) 1.8×10³ N/C toward the −2.0 nC charge; 1.8×10² V
C. 9.0×10² N/C toward the −2.0 nC charge; 1.8×10² V
D. 1.8×10³ N/C toward the −2.0 nC charge; 3.6×10² V

stem: Two positive point charges, +1.0 µC and +9.0 µC, are fixed 0.80 m apart on the x-axis in vacuum. Take V = 0 at infinity. At the point between them where the net electric field is zero, what are its distance from the +1.0 µC charge and the electric potential there?

A solid insulating sphere of radius R carries charge distributed uniformly throughout its volume. The electric field magnitude at the surface of the sphere is E_s. What is the field magnitude at a distance R/3 from the center?

A long solid insulating cylinder of radius 0.040 m carries a uniform volume charge density ρ = 3.0 µC/m³. Far from its ends, what is the electric field magnitude at a distance of 0.020 m from its axis? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)

A solid insulating sphere of radius R = 0.20 m has a volume charge density that increases linearly with distance from the center, ρ(r) = ρ₀(r/R), where ρ₀ = 8.0 µC/m³. What is the electric field magnitude at r = 0.10 m? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)
A solid copper sphere is given an excess charge and then left isolated until all charges are at rest. Where is the excess charge located?
criteria: A. Concentrated at the center of the sphere
B. Half on the surface and half in the interior
C. (correct) Entirely on the outer surface
D. Spread uniformly throughout the volume

stem: A neutral, thick conducting spherical shell has a +5.0 nC point charge at the center of its hollow cavity. The system is in electrostatic equilibrium. What charge is on the shell's inner surface and what charge is on its outer surface?
criteria: A. Inner surface 0; outer surface +5.0 nC
B. (correct) Inner surface −5.0 nC; outer surface +5.0 nC
C. Inner surface −5.0 nC; outer surface 0

stem: A point charge of +5.0 nC sits at the center of a thick conducting spherical shell with inner radius 0.10 m and outer radius 0.20 m. The shell carries a net charge of −3.0 nC and is in electrostatic equilibrium. What are the electric field magnitudes at r = 0.15 m (inside the conducting material) and at r = 0.30 m, with the direction at r = 0.30 m?
criteria: B. (correct) At 0.15 m: 0; at 0.30 m: 2.0×10² N/C radially outward
C. At 0.15 m: 0; at 0.30 m: 5.0×10² N/C radially outward
D. At 0.15 m: 2.0×10³ N/C; at 0.30 m: 2.0×10² N/C, both radially outward

stem: A point charge of +9.0 nC is at the center of a cube. What is the electric flux through two opposite faces of the cube taken together? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)
A point charge is at the center of a cube. The electric flux through one face of the cube is 150 N·m²/C. What is the value of the charge? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)

An imaginary hemispherical dome of radius 0.30 m rests on a flat circular base. A +5.0 nC point charge is at the center of the base, so the field is radial. What is the electric flux through the curved dome alone? (ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)
